name: Wi-Fi

claims.claim_text: Battery operation and Wi-Fi are in direct conflict: a battery-powered Wi-Fi device is designed around turning the radio off and sleeping whenever it is not transmitting, so the design question becomes how rarely the device can afford to wake.
claims.quote_verbatim: turning off wifi and going to a sleep state when you're not doing anything
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: Measured current on a small Wi-Fi module spans two orders of magnitude by state: one to two milliamps with the radio off, five to six milliamps connected in power-save mode, and about one hundred milliamps with everything on.
claims.quote_verbatim: on with wifi on in power save is five or six
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi and cellular have opposite transmit-power incentives. Under LTE a handset lowers its output so the base station can just hear it, while a Wi-Fi station wants every node in the cell to hear it and therefore transmits at maximum power, which is why Wi-Fi power budgets do not shrink with proximity to the access point.
claims.quote_verbatim: in Wi-Fi, it's actually sort of the opposite, which is you want everybody to hear you when you're talking
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: Consumer routers implement behaviour the Wi-Fi specification forbids, such as accepting a zero-length password, so a connected product has to tolerate router defects rather than assume conformance.
claims.quote_verbatim: things that are specifically forbidden in the spec for Wi-Fi, some routers just implement
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: The catalogue of router interoperability defects can only be assembled from a large deployed fleet: half a million shipped modules across thirty to forty countries produced connection data no individual small company could gather for itself, which is the argument for buying a connectivity platform rather than writing the link layer in-house.
claims.quote_verbatim: tested on so many different networks
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: Getting a device onto Wi-Fi is the easy part of a connected product; the sustained work is the service behind it, which is why connectivity vendors sell the backend rather than the radio.
claims.quote_verbatim: I like to think of it more as an internet module than as a Wi-Fi module
claims.speaker: Brandon Harris
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Brandon Harris - Impish Internet Iamatology

claims.claim_text: A low-cost Wi-Fi module draws two hundred to three hundred milliamps at peak and under one milliwatt in deep sleep, so average consumption is set almost entirely by duty cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: 200 to 300 milliamps peak power
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi transmit bursts are supplied from bulk decoupling rather than drawn through the cell: heavy bypass capacitance smooths the peak so the current does not have to pass through the battery's equivalent series resistance.
claims.quote_verbatim: you smooth it out with your, you know, some heavy bypass
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi is high power relative to Bluetooth Low Energy and low power only relative to always-on Wi-Fi devices, so the comparison class has to be stated before calling a Wi-Fi part low power.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you're comparing it to Bluetooth low energy, then it's high power, but relative to other Wi-Fi devices that are always on, it's low power
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Wearables Might Have Limited Fashion Options - Lachrymogenic Lane Language

claims.claim_text: In a sensor network, a hub-and-spoke topology of low-power proprietary radio nodes feeding one Wi-Fi gateway consumes less total power than putting Wi-Fi on every node, even though the hub then runs two radio solutions; twenty nodes is enough for the aggregate to favour the two-radio design.
claims.quote_verbatim: that solution would be in aggregate higher power than having 20 of the low-power RF nodes
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: The reason not to put Wi-Fi on every leaf node is cost and, increasingly, power alone: a battery-powered leaf node cannot carry Wi-Fi at a usable service life.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't battery power the node with Wi-Fi
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: The gateway problem disappears when the low-power radio is built into the router, because the router is the one always-powered internet hub already present at every site; an extra translating bridge is another mains-powered box to install and maintain.
claims.quote_verbatim: It has to be built into the router because the router is the internet hub of every home
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: A protocol carried into a router has to stay simple enough to run in a couple of kilobytes on a three-dollar device and to be usable at hundred-piece volumes, not just at hundred-thousand-piece volumes, or the low-power tier never materialises.
claims.quote_verbatim: it should run on, you know, a couple K of code on these embedded devices so that they can cost $3
claims.speaker: Luke Beno
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Luke Beno of Analog.io

claims.claim_text: The 2.4 GHz band is unsuitable for mission-critical control links at public venues because every phone and access point in the room occupies it; wireless stage costumes running on 2.4 GHz suffered unexplained random signal drops until the band itself was identified as the cause.
claims.quote_verbatim: 2.4 gigahertz is not a good band to be in
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: A domestic Wi-Fi router radiates on the order of two hundred milliwatts, which sets the interference floor other 2.4 GHz devices in the same space have to work against.
claims.quote_verbatim: Wi-Fi routers are, like, like, 200 milliwatts
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi's only serious disadvantage for home devices is power consumption, and where the device is mains-powered and the network already exists, that disadvantage does not apply, which is what makes cheap Wi-Fi modules the default for fixed indoor products.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only problem with Wi-Fi is that it's power hungry. But if you're in, like, a home scenario, then you don't really care that much about power
claims.speaker: Akiba
claims.episode_title: An interview with Akiba from Freaklabs - Dimissory Diagraphical Debt

claims.claim_text: Amplitude-only demodulation in the 2.4 GHz band is highly vulnerable to interference from Wi-Fi traffic; a live radio-reflection demonstration failed outright in a room holding fifteen hundred people, and the remedy pursued was direct-sequence spread spectrum modulation to recover the signal from the interferers.
claims.quote_verbatim: the demo totally failed. And I think the reason that it failed was actually due to RF interference
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching With Charvat And Ossmann - Recurring RF Remontados

claims.claim_text: Range at fixed power is a function of frequency: moving below one gigahertz buys range that 2.4 GHz cannot reach without more power, and the sub-gigahertz FSK stack is far simpler than a Wi-Fi stack, so both range and software complexity push long-link designs off Wi-Fi.
claims.quote_verbatim: to get more range, you're going to have to look at lower frequencies
claims.speaker: Felix Rusu

claims.claim_text: Regulatory limits on access-point transmit power of a few hundred milliwatts exist to protect other receivers from being blinded and to keep the shared band usable, not because of any exposure hazard at those levels.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's because it will blind other receivers
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian

claims.claim_text: Reverse-polarity antenna connectors on Wi-Fi equipment exist because United States regulators objected that a standard connector would let a user swap the supplied antenna for a high-gain Yagi and extend coverage well beyond the intended area; the non-standard gender is a compliance device, not an electrical one.
claims.quote_verbatim: What's keeping the consumer from removing your antenna and putting a Yagi antenna there with the same connector?
claims.episode_title: All the Connectors with Davide Andrea

claims.claim_text: Millimetre-wave links do not pass through walls and beam steering does not fix that, so a millimetre-wave replacement for Wi-Fi implies an access point in every room.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not going to go through a wall
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi has occupied both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz for over a decade, so an antenna design for a Wi-Fi product must cover both bands rather than one.
claims.quote_verbatim: wifi is at least for the last 10 years, always 2.4 and five gig
claims.speaker: Pete Bevilacqua

claims.claim_text: In handsets, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi typically share one radio and one antenna, while GPS at 1.575 GHz either has its own antenna or shares with Wi-Fi or cellular; the antenna engineer works from the band list rather than the protocol names.
claims.quote_verbatim: typically on these phones, Bluetooth and wifi share the same radio and the same antenna
claims.speaker: Pete Bevilacqua

claims.claim_text: Line-of-sight range figures do not predict deployed performance: a radio that reaches five hundred feet in the open may not cross ten feet of concrete wall, so range testing has to be done in the intended environment.
claims.quote_verbatim: just because the radio can get 500 feet. Doesn't mean your radio will get 10 feet through a concrete wall
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: Networked products routinely work in the development office and fail in the operating environment, because the office has a fibre backhaul and clear spectrum while the deployment site may sit among twenty-five overlapping Wi-Fi networks; testing difficult radio scenarios deliberately is the missing step.
claims.quote_verbatim: works great in the office. You put it into the actual operating environment and then it doesn't function at all
claims.speaker: Phillip Johnston
claims.episode_title: Firmware for Hardware Engineers with Phillip Johnston

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi run at its lowest coding rates, using the one-megabit schemes and vendor long-range modes, reaches roughly eight hundred metres, which puts it in competition with dedicated long-range radio for many links.
claims.quote_verbatim: around 800 meters is kind of like where the sorts of stuff that I do with wifi kind of top out
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: For point-to-point data between microcontrollers, the connectionless ESP-NOW mode of Espressif parts is used in preference to an ordinary Wi-Fi association, because it removes the access point from the path.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm just using like ESP now with Espressif chips
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: Real-time audio work will not tolerate Wi-Fi: delays of tens of milliseconds are audible in a two-way recorded conversation, so a wired connection is used for the link that carries the audio.
claims.quote_verbatim: tens of milliseconds matter
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi is engineered for throughput rather than bounded latency, so a fast, predictable round trip is not something it will ever provide.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's never going to be like, oh, quick ping and deterministic type stuff
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Industrial and SCADA installations resist wireless because their control loops treat any packet loss as unacceptable and retries as a hazard, which is a requirements position rather than a preference.
claims.quote_verbatim: any amount of packet loss is not really allowed
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Against the industrial preference for wire, a radio designer with field experience holds that a modern Wi-Fi link is often more reliable than an RS-485 bus, not because the wire is at fault but because RS-485 has many implementations and many ways to be got wrong, whereas the wireless stack is monolithic and well tested.
claims.quote_verbatim: in many cases they're wireless would have been more reliable than RS45
claims.speaker: J.P. Norair

claims.claim_text: A product that relies on the customer's existing Wi-Fi inherits that infrastructure: field installations are commonly a consumer router in a closet on its default SSID and password, shared with everyone on the premises, down much of the time and knocked off the air by nearby switching equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is a old links, this router in the closet with like the default SSID and password
claims.speaker: Eli Hughes

claims.claim_text: The argument that Wi-Fi is free does not survive deployment: someone pays for data eventually, and the engineering and support cost of using a site's Wi-Fi is what pushed one instrumentation product from Wi-Fi to a cellular link.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going to pay for data at some point
claims.speaker: Eli Hughes

claims.claim_text: Cellular backhaul is chosen over site Wi-Fi partly to avoid the customer's IT department: an industrial sensor product shipped its first deployment entirely on 3G because plant networks are not opened to new devices.
claims.quote_verbatim: for the initial deployment, we did everything with 3G and were able to bypass plant IT
claims.speaker: Gerry Roston

claims.claim_text: A common industrial architecture puts battery leaf nodes on 802.15.4 and makes the mains-powered gateway the only device that carries the site uplink, with Wi-Fi or cellular fitted to the gateway as a build option.
claims.quote_verbatim: we can either slot in Wi-Fi or 3G into our product
claims.speaker: Gerry Roston

claims.claim_text: Utility customers reject Wi-Fi as a data path on reliability grounds, which constrains metering and energy-monitoring products that transmit over the householder's network.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's too unreliable for us. We can't, we couldn't possibly use wifi

claims.claim_text: The standard way a headless device joins a network is to open its own temporary access point so a phone can hand over the household credentials, which is why a newly installed appliance appears as an open SSID.
claims.quote_verbatim: A lot of times it'll open up a little wifi AP and that's how you hand it over the credentials to your network

claims.claim_text: Security risk scoring ranks attack vectors from remote through local and adjacent to physical, where radio protocols including Wi-Fi and Bluetooth count as adjacent; once a device holds an IP address on a Linux stack it moves up that scale because network-reachable attack surface scores higher than RF-adjacent surface.
claims.quote_verbatim: And then you have adjacent, which is a lot of times where us IOT security researchers live

claims.claim_text: Provisioning can be moved off Wi-Fi entirely: giving the product a cellular path lets the owner enter network credentials in an app rather than making the installer hop onto the device's access point and back, which removes a step that costs installer time on every unit.
claims.quote_verbatim: the homeowner can open their app and plug in wi-fi credentials
claims.speaker: Kerry Scharfglass

claims.claim_text: A connected controller must keep its primary function when the network is gone: a Wi-Fi thermostat that loses its server or its association falls back to its local sensor and continues to regulate temperature, degraded but working, because the appliance function cannot be allowed to depend on the link.
claims.quote_verbatim: it will just rely exclusively on its internal sensor
claims.speaker: Keith Burzinski
claims.episode_title: Automating the Home with Keith Burzinski

claims.claim_text: Interactive products built on Wi-Fi round trips inherit the link's latency, so a device expected to respond immediately should not put the response path over the network.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of the products that are coming out, they're just Wi-Fi connected. And then they expect to be responsive
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi modules carry a dedicated processor for the protocol stack because running the stack on the application microcontroller leaves too few resources for the application itself; the host then talks to the module over SPI, I2C or a serial link.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a reason why those Wi-Fi modules have their own dedicated processing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Hamvention, Arduino and Intel - Burdensome Background Battology

claims.claim_text: The ESP8266 put a Wi-Fi radio and a 32-bit Tensilica processor on a board selling for about two dollars seventy, a price point that changed which products could justify a network connection.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're looking at a device that costs now about $2.70 for a board
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Espressif shipped a complete development environment as a downloadable virtual machine with compilers and full source, which is what let users go past the intended use of the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've given you a full development environment
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: The ESP8266 was designed as a serial peripheral driven by AT commands from a host microcontroller, and users deleted the host, running the application on the processor already inside the radio chip, for compactness and lower power.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting rid of the microcontroller externally and they're using the one that's right on the chip itself
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: Engineers will accept a clumsy interface, in this case AT commands over a serial port, when the part is cheap enough, and will build the missing tooling themselves; low cost from the bottom of the market is the repeated pattern by which such parts displace established ones.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going to use the AT commands to connect to it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Documentation access decided the outcome among contemporaries: rival low-cost Asian Wi-Fi silicon of the same period never released usable documentation and went nowhere, while the equivalent parts from established western vendors were far more expensive.
claims.quote_verbatim: their stuff didn't leak. And so they weren't able to make it right
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi crossed a threshold when a module reached five dollars and then when a single sub-dollar part combined the microcontroller and the radio, at which point adding connectivity stopped needing a justification in the bill of materials.
claims.quote_verbatim: now it's a sub dollar part that you can go include on your schematic
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: The initial data sheet for the part that opened up cheap Wi-Fi was readable only by native Chinese speakers, and a user community translated it before the chip could be used widely; before that, adding Wi-Fi to a product was either hard or expensive or both.
claims.quote_verbatim: a data sheet that could only be read by native Chinese speakers
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: By the mid-2010s the planning assumption for a connected product had inverted, with a Linux-capable computer, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth all treated as free at the board level and the design effort moved elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: Assume that a Linux computer is free. Assume that Wi-Fi is free.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Shifting Away From DIY - Pedetentious PnP Progress

claims.claim_text: Earlier, integrating Wi-Fi was expensive enough to take a large share of a product's bill of materials, the same cost trajectory later travelled by other integrated sensing technologies.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was so expensive to integrate Wi-Fi
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The ESP32 pairs two 240 MHz 32-bit cores running FreeRTOS with classic Bluetooth, Bluetooth Low Energy and Wi-Fi that supports both station and access-point modes as well as scanning.
claims.quote_verbatim: 240 megahertz, 32 bit processors
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: A Wi-Fi microcontroller can run either as a station joining an existing network or as an access point that other devices join, and the two modes serve different product roles: pulling data from the internet versus offering a local configuration network.
claims.quote_verbatim: it can act as an access point
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Later parts moved the same integration onto RISC-V and added the second band, giving low-cost chips that serve both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz networks.
claims.quote_verbatim: the new ESP32C5 is a RISC-V based Wi-Fi and Bluetooth processor
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Wow, Dave REALLY likes Top Gun

claims.claim_text: A measured throughput figure for a low-cost Wi-Fi microcontroller board is about five megabits per second, which bounds what such a part can be asked to carry.
claims.quote_verbatim: got five megabits to his wifi
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Cloning a Wi-Fi system-on-chip is not a matter of copying silicon: clones of complex parts are behavioural reimplementations, and reproducing a Wi-Fi and Bluetooth chip means working from the standards and building the radio processing afresh.
claims.quote_verbatim: we looked at the wi-fi standard then we looked at the bluetooth standard
claims.speaker: Jeroen Domburg

claims.claim_text: Anyone with access to a Wi-Fi network is in a position to reach every computer on it and to keep that access after leaving radio range, so network membership should be treated as equivalent to physical access.
claims.quote_verbatim: somebody who's on your Wi-Fi, is very likely able to gain access to every computer on your network
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: The KRACK weakness in WPA2 applied to essentially every Wi-Fi router and every Wi-Fi-connected device in the field, a class of exposure that patching cannot fully close because much of the installed base never receives updates.
claims.quote_verbatim: there was a huge WPA2 vulnerability. Which is used on every router
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Because Wi-Fi maintains association state, an attacker can forge disconnection messages so that station and access point each believe the other has gone, then impersonate the station; protocols with no connected or disconnected state are not open to that attack and can only be jammed.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's some kind of attack you could not do with Laura because there is no connected or disconnected state
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A consumer drone controlled over Wi-Fi without authentication can be taken over by deauthenticating the owner and connecting in their place; a single-board computer with a wireless card carried on a second drone performed this in flight and chained the captured aircraft into a following swarm.
claims.quote_verbatim: deauthenticate them, connect as the owner
claims.speaker: Samy Kamkar

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi doubles as a positioning system: a device reports the access points it can see and a database of network identifiers returns a position, which is faster than a satellite fix and works indoors.
claims.quote_verbatim: looking up which wifi networks it sees and says, Oh, you're probably here
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A part may carry a Wi-Fi radio purely for identifier-based location rather than as a general network interface, so the presence of Wi-Fi in a device's block diagram does not imply it can carry data.
claims.quote_verbatim: It doesn't have Wi-Fi generically as a Wi-Fi interface. It's just part of the location mapping
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi is chosen over Bluetooth when content has to be pushed to a device, because Bluetooth's practical ceiling of about one megabit per second or less limits how much can be sent, and a device with little local compute depends on receiving rendered content over the link.
claims.quote_verbatim: having a practical limit of one megabit per second or less for throughput
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: Where a wearable must hold a Wi-Fi link on a single lithium cell, the module is selected for its sleep-mode behaviour rather than its active performance.
claims.quote_verbatim: it has good sleep modes and low power consumption in the sleep modes
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: Thread was built to reuse the 802.15.4 radios already shipping in Zigbee products, forming a self-healing mesh that is a separate backbone from Wi-Fi, cellular and Ethernet and sits just above IP networking so higher-level protocols can run on top of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'd actually use the same radio that was found in Zigbee
claims.speaker: Jonathan Beri
claims.episode_title: Why IoT Is Difficult with Jonathan Beri

claims.claim_text: Structured cabling should be installed during construction because pulling new wire into a finished building is expensive and the opportunity does not return, and because Wi-Fi does not cover every case.
claims.quote_verbatim: put in some Cat 6. You're not going to get a chance again
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Streaming continuous instrument data over a wireless link runs into the same problem as wired networking, only worse: neither Wi-Fi nor Ethernet is deterministic, and a transport that guarantees eventual delivery does not guarantee timely delivery.
claims.quote_verbatim: streaming data is always a problem even if it's connected by you know two gigabit ethernet ports
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Headless Units and Baseless Batteries - KiCad Kickoff Kopophobia

claims.claim_text: Dense venues degrade Wi-Fi through sheer user count rather than through any equipment fault, which is why conference and hotel networks fail for work that assumes a stable link.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's just because there's so many people in an area
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: 3D Printed Shark Jumps - Edifying Edison's Energy

claims.claim_text: Any product emitting in the 2.4 GHz band shares it with the customer's own network, so a design that interferes with nearby Wi-Fi creates a support problem regardless of whether it meets emissions limits.
claims.quote_verbatim: everything spews 2.4 gigahertz
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A typical Wi-Fi board is manufactured in volume on ordinary FR4, so guidance to reach for a low-dielectric-constant PTFE laminate on a 2.4 GHz design mistakes the requirements of high-performance RF for the requirements of consumer wireless.
claims.quote_verbatim: you mean like for a wifi board, the one that they build millions of on FR4
claims.speaker: Zachariah Peterson

claims.claim_text: A vendor without a Wi-Fi part of its own adds connectivity by placing a third-party Wi-Fi module alongside its microcontroller and driving it in AT-command mode, which is why development boards pair an unrelated radio chip with the host processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: There's an ESP32 module that they're using with AT mode just to give it Wi-Fi
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Harvesting usable energy from ambient Wi-Fi is not practical: charging a phone battery from a Wi-Fi signal works out at something like twenty-six years.
claims.quote_verbatim: It would take 26 years or something to charge the battery
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Demonstrations of powering devices over Wi-Fi depend on a modified access point transmitting continuously at full power rather than on ordinary network traffic, so the result does not transfer to a standard router.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have to get a special wifi router that had special firmware that was modified to always continuously transmit it the full one watt power
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Consolidate All The Things - Zonked Zelotic Zaitech

claims.claim_text: Radiated power from a fixed transmitter falls with the square of distance, so separation is the effective control on exposure, and an access point's transmit power can also be reduced in its own settings when coverage allows.
claims.quote_verbatim: It drops with a square of the distance
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Texas Instruments, OPA & Chevy Volt - Nerdy Neuroelectronic Neurosis

claims.claim_text: Enclosing a router in a metal cage blocks the signal it is there to provide; where transmitted power is genuinely a concern the setting can be lowered in the access point's configuration.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can go into the Wi-Fi settings and adjust the power level
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian

claims.claim_text: A retired router can be repurposed as an access point fed by an Ethernet drop to fix a coverage dead zone, and an 802.11n unit delivering around fifty megabits per second is sufficient for streamed video.
claims.quote_verbatim: I took my old Wi-Fi 4 router, which is 802.11n, and I, you know, went through the settings and I repurposed it and made it into an access point
claims.speaker: Martin Rowe
claims.episode_title: The Measurement Blues with Martin Rowe

claims.claim_text: Wi-Fi and the broadband modem together can account for around sixteen watts of continuous household draw, eight watts each, which is significant for always-on equipment.
claims.quote_verbatim: They were like eight each or something. Eight watts each
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Adding Wi-Fi to a small single-board computer raises its idle consumption measurably; the wireless variant of one board idles higher than the equivalent board without it, with a reported figure of about 260 milliamps.
claims.quote_verbatim: they saw 260 milliamps idle
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Embedded Linux earns its place when a system has to combine several subsystems at once, such as Wi-Fi with a camera and Ethernet; implementing Wi-Fi on a microcontroller that does not integrate the radio is impractical enough that the integrated part effectively decides the architecture.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need wifi and a camera and ethernet

claims.claim_text: Shipping a fleet of Wi-Fi devices creates obligations beyond the radio: firmware has to be updated across every unit in the field, the fleet's state has to be visible, and data return has to be verified, which is the service that connectivity platforms exist to provide.
claims.quote_verbatim: How do I then go in update firmware on all of them?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Cellular data costs recur where Wi-Fi appears free to the end user, which is the recurring commercial objection to cellular-connected products even when the radio itself is cheap.
claims.quote_verbatim: people have to pay for their data when they're used to like, Hey, I have an ESP 32. I can just hook it into wifi
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Cellular network generations are switched off while products are still in service, stranding devices whose only uplink was that generation; Wi-Fi capability in the same device is what keeps it working, so the choice of uplink is a product-lifetime decision.
claims.quote_verbatim: a lot of 3G shutting down
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: In the mid-2000s the only thing Wi-Fi was used for was replacing the Ethernet cable on a laptop, and the design premise behind the first wall-mounted Wi-Fi appliances was that the same radio could deliver web content to a fixed device, a premise settled a year later when the smartphone arrived.
